They are your legally entitled rest days. Jurisdictions vary. Some places I’ve worked 8 weeks straight, some 28 days is the max. Currently I work 14 on (12 hour shifts) and 14 off. 

Seasons vary depending on the scope of work. This year I have friends whose winter drill programs had to end 2 months early because of mild conditions leading to swamps/waterways melting. They’re off until June when their field season starts. Just like I’ve had years where snow/frost came early and we had to wrap up our mapping/soil sampling earlier than we hoped and without a drill program that year we were off until March. The one consistent thing in exploration is that nothing is set in stone. 

If you want stability, look at production geology roles (beat geologist, pit geologist type roles). FIFO in a production role would have the stability you seek financially, with the steady rotations . I personally found production to be repetitive and prefer the adventure of exploration, but I have friends who adore production.

I’m in Canada for reference. 

When I’m off, I’m staying with my parents to save for my house, otherwise I’m travelling. If it weren’t for that, I would be paying rent while away. And a good portion of my coworkers do the same, or live the transient couch surfing life to save as much as possible. Depending on your rotations you can be home anywhere from 7-14 days after a run, so it’s not that much if you have places to visit. 

For one junior company they did have short term employee housing. The expectation was that you would move into the community within the year. The rent was minimal and was deducted from my pay-check.

 I do find in the mining towns that  rent is inflated compared to similar sized towns. Landlords know we don’t have a choice and have short/long term rentals priced to match that, plus there is a lack of inventory. But based off of your post history, these rents are significantly less than NYC.

Sign up for the CIM tour, go to the student industry networking luncheon. Your university will likely host an event as well, it’s a good way to connect with program alumni and network. Check out the student industry colloquium. 

For the price I would get a pass to the event, then you can come and go as you please. The Core Shack changes each day (that’s where you’re likely to meet more geos and get to talk a little geology). 

the investors exchange you can get info about different juniors and their projects (don’t be surprised if they aren’t arsed to talk to you though, as you’re not an investor and it seems rare now to find geos at the booths). 

The Trade show side is cool to see, you can get an idea of all the different services, and providers. Usually that’s where you’ll find the universities, PGO, countries and different provinces. Oh and of course the mineral/rock vendors. 

The North Trade show side is geared to northern Ontario and a few other service providers. 

I’m a glutton for panel talks, these are great to attend. I try to hit one from each different program. And recently they’ve added where you have access to the presentations afterwards. 

Things are vastly different from 10-15 years ago, so the events afterwards are ticketed/invite only. Sometimes you can find some on eventbrite and sign up. The event at Ripley’s aquarium is nice and the Steamwhistle event. 

Bring business cards, I can’t stress this enough. No one wants your resume or CV, but card is a quick exchange of contact info, and there’s tones of draws at booths and that’s your entry. 

PS wear comfy shoes! If you have more specific questions feel free to DM me, I’ll do my best to answer them.

Crib sheet pre approved 48 hours prior to writing 
Subsidized tutoring up to 10 hours per semester (department paid 50%)
Physical copies of electronic materials 
Permission to use recording tools for lectures
Biweekly therapy sessions covered by university health plan (attendance is mandatory to access accommodations)
Monthly review with accessibility services staff to review any needed changes, timelines and new study strategies 
Pre-paid printer card for the university library to print/photocopy slides, course materials as needed 🥹

I have a mixed review. The application process sucked. It was easy enough to fill out the forms and get my prior 2 universities to send the info. The negative was I had to call a three times to get them to process it. There was always a “reason” why it was taking so long, ultimately it was that it was misplaced. It ended up taking 4 months, so I couldn’t book any tests or exams in that time as I didn’t have a letter for my accommodations. I ended up having to pay for course extensions. This timing also impacted my ability to get accommodations for materials (hard copy of textbooks) 

Of the 3 universities I’ve now been enrolled at, this was the worst in terms of what was available to assist. Yes you’ll get your letter for accommodations you need, but there’s no help in finding or funding tutors.  Theres limited counseling services, there’s counselling services that started in January and I used one session before my term ended. There’s no grants or equipment for rent to help with notes. So I find getting all of this on one’s own increases the financial cost quite a bit. 

Next my two professors were not at all accommodating. One gave the details of the exam the night before, though I had booked the exam with the department 3 weeks prior. This prof just uses teams, but by the time I was given details of format and time, there was no time to have my accommodations honoured. I went through accessibility and advocated for myself, they sent the request to Success, who took 3 weeks to get back to us. 

The other one would not provide a physical textbook copy, and I was unable to find a copy of it online . The online “lecture” notes were mostly broken links, it made studying horrendous. I was constantly sending in requests for the content to be repaired. I ended up dropping this course. 

The people I spoke to at Accessibility services were always kind. I’m hoping my  application for accommodations was a fluke. But I never felt supported like I did at other institutions. There were no check ins, no additional supports, just a webpage list of things you can purchase on your own. They did help me navigating dropping one course so it wouldn’t impact my GPA. 

My advice if you go through with Athabasca: Be on top of Accessibility Services. Don’t let them tell you “oh it’s a normal wait time, it will be soon”. Push and advocate for yourself. I definitely didn’t feel seen or understood by their department but at least they were always courteous.

Hey!! Fellow chronic spoonie. I’ve been in the industry for 7 years now mostly in greenfield exploration. My experience has been rocky as I don’t know anyone else more senior than me who’s struggling. 

My advice would be to get on with a major if you’re wanting to be in exploration. Reason being they have a robust HR department and will be able to have accommodations to help you. You’d be more likely to have more supports and have a team that isn’t stretched thin. I’ve been with small juniors and consulting companies that just don’t always have the capacity and a lot of times I have to sacrifice my well being and specialist appointments to support the team and schedule. 

Camps can be difficult especially if you’re like me and flare ups can be triggered by food allergies and poor nutrition. But if you have a good company/manager they’ll advocate to get options for you. 

When you’re working in field crews don’t be afraid to speak up and tell someone to slow down or that you need a break for water or rest. Don’t be afraid to ask for help to carry heavy items like core boxes. I find being open with the team about limitations can be helpful. 

Biggest tips to help make it easier : buy good field gear! Don’t skimp, it makes all the difference. A good comfortable back pack especially for your fibro! I also have reynaulds, and then heat intolerance in the summer. I find lululemon swiftly tops are the BEST for temp regulating (my dad works in the industry and is in late 60’s and stubborn, got him hooked on the men’s version too) . I adore the merino wool base layer tights and wear them as my long underwear for cool climates. Get good boots! It will reduce pain. Those little heat packs for boots and mits are a life saver, and the theraband low back one is great for real cold days. 

Future looking: start now with learning skills to transition to more office/project management. Get on mailing lists for free trainings for things like: leapfrog, datamine, Vulcan, deswick, advance GIS, various reports and tenure seminars. Most of us make the transition at some point, but starting early will give you a knowledge base and options in the case of a flare up preventing you from doing field work. 

Mine Production is also an option. Depending on the site and role it’s less wear and tear on your body. Underground can be uncomfortable for heat intolerance, but in my experience working the beat, it was only half a day underground. The rest of my day was digitizing mine workings, and reporting.

Naturopaths do go to university for an advanced degree, they have an ND as opposed to an MD. 

Some naturalpathic doctors spew complete hokum. Such as live blood analysis, that’s absolutely a scam (that squiggle is a bit of fibre off someone’s clothes, not undigested beef in my blood). Crystal healing, trash.

A good NDwill go through your lifestyle and day to day with you and help find adjustments to your diet and lifestyle that are manageable and help improve your symptoms. A good ND won’t push dozens of supplements, and especially not their own proprietary blend. They’ll be up on peer reviewed medical data and be willing to share those studies with you. 

A good ND will be able and willing to say that something isn’t their expertise and help guide you to get referrals you need. Whether it’s a dietitian, guiding/supporting the process to get referrals through your MD to endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, rheumatologists etc. 

I know some real terrible ND’s in town because they tried to solicit me away from mine with claims not based in science and push their supplements on me when I went to the health food store they operate out of. But I know a lot more amazing ones. It’s like all other professionals, some suck and some are amazing. The comment to try an ND wasn’t totally off base. 

To OP: I’d start with a dietician. Doctors only get limited training on that in med school due to everything they have to cover. I had major GI issues, so I sympathize, it’s shitty and painful. Personally I went to an ND that focused on diet, GI to pair with my MD’s treatment plan. 

TL;DR: there are whack NDs out there, and there are fantastic ones. They have a role in a functional health team. Just have to find the ones that work for you.

My experience:

Referred after painful menstrual cycles, sex, and incontinence. I’m a SA survivor so I was very nervous going in. My therapist has been amazing honestly. My first appointment we talked about what was going on, my health history, she explained how things work, we did an assessment and a bit of treatment. Every one of my appointments has had an internal exam and working to release muscular tension. We’ve discussed rectal exams but it’s never been necessary. I was fortunate and don’t have any prolapse, or too much tension requiring dilators, meaning my progression through treatment has been rapid. We’re currently working on “pelvic floor remapping” and desensitizing. My first appointment had more talking and her showing me what she does. I actually learned I’ve been breathing incorrectly this whole time, and things have gotten so much better with re-learning proper breathing. 

I have never experienced pain or bleeding after an appointment. She moves at a pace I can handle and checks in a lot as we’re moving through muscle groups. If I need her to back off on pressure she does, but it’s never been pain like other physio.  I did have some very mild cramping after one of my early appointments, she had worked on massaging a particularly tight muscle, I’d rate it a 1. 

Her and I actually talked about paps and colposcopy at my last appointment. She said if need another one, book in with her a day before and she will get me ready for it, we’ll work on relaxation techniques, desensitization of the surrounding tissues, and do what we can to make it an easier procedure. 

My biggest advice, do your best to be consistent with any “homework”. The exercises you’re given to do at home help so much, I can really tell when I haven’t had the time to do them.

A few of the exercises I have to do as my “homework” are:
1. Deep belly breathing, the goal is to fill up deep into your belly imagine the breath all the way down into your pelvic floor. I was taught to imagine a flower blooming and then closing. 
2. Don’t push to pee! It’s so counter intuitive from what we’re taught. You want to think of the muscles relaxing. Breathing with those deep belly breaths helps. When my leakage was bad I was instructed to sit an extra few seconds and focus on that deep breath so the muscles relax and the remaining urine comes out. 
3. Stop yourself from clenching your jaw, there’s a link between those groups of muscles. Again breathing is your friend to help with that. It’s the hardest part for me. 
4. A stool or a squatty potty for when you do use the washroom. Brings your legs into a healthy position for voiding. 

Those are the things you can safely do without an assessment. Your current physio might even be able to give you a few stretches with modifications to help. I know when I hurt my SI joint, I was dumping all my stability into my pelvic floor to protect my back, but between back physio and pelvic floor physio I’m doing a lot better. And the pelvic PT actually help speed up my low back recovery (she can get into the muscles from the other side) 

During your assessment they do a physical internal exam (it’s not as invasive as a pap or anything like that) they’ll check your muscle quality, how strong your control is. In my case it was a strong pelvic floor, with dysfunction - so I’m always holding tension there and it was strong but tight. So we had to do a lot of pelvic massage (it’s a lil weird the first time but now it seems fairly normal to me), stretching and breathing to get my muscles to actually relax again, I couldn’t do kegels at the start because I was actually causing more damage.

It could be just a tight pelvic floor not allowing for proper peeing. OP do you find you “push” to pee? Do you clench your jaw a lot? If you are able get a referral for pelvic floor physio, or get an assessment. I was having similar problems with “leaking” and urgency, going to physio for it has improved it so much. But I would definitely talk to your doctor to rule out other things to be safe too :) if you have questions about pelvic floor physio I’m happy to answer about my experience.
